newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe industry says budget a missed opportunity.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe industry says budget a missed opportunity.

text.p: The Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries (CZI) said the government had missed an opportunity in a budget unveiled on Thursday to buttress efforts to boost foreign investment and economic growth.

CZI chief executive Joe Foroma, describing the 18-month budget presented by Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa as unexciting, said the budget deficit forecast for 1998 was still too high at 8.9 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
"There's nothing in the budget to really cause us excitement," Foroma told Reuters.

"We think that having had some growth in the economy last year and with all the initiatives we are currently making to market the country as an investment destination, the budget ought to have been an instrument to buttress those efforts," he said.

"The budget deficit is still too high...The government is going to be borrowing big from the domestic market and that will fuel inflationary pressures which gives the prognosis for high interest rates in the foreseeable future," he added.

Murerwa pegged the spending deficit for the financial year ended June 30 at 7.1 percent of GDP, way below an earlier figure of 10.3 of GDP he gave to Reuters earlier in the month which was off a government-set target of 8.5 percent.

He attributed the surprise reduction to improved revenue collection, proceeds from the privatisation of the national dairy, Dairibord, and proceeds totalling Z$1 billion from the central Reserve Bank.
Murerwa forecast government borrowing from the domestic market as a percentage of GDP to rise to 6.7 percent of GDP from six percent in 1996/97.

Local economists, Western donors and industrialists have in the past blamed high government borrowing from the local market for contributing to a widening budget deficit and keeping annual inflation and interest rates high.

Foroma said Murerwa's pledges to bring down annual inflation to 16.5 percent by next June from 21.4 percent last June and a further lower to 12 percent by year end were ambitious unless the government followed up the statements of intent with concrete action, particularly to speed up its privatisation programme.

However, some market analysts said the budget was positive and was likely to cheer the stock exchange which has been trading firmly for the past two weeks until Wednesday when it started coming off ahead of Thursday's announcement.

Remo Pollastri, a director with economic and market analysts Dataworld said Murerwa's optimism over Zimbabwe's prospects of securing a resumption of Western donor aid for further economic reforms would boost sentiment on the market.
